short_summary: Solitude was historically seen as a warning sign
Psychology treated solitude as a symptom or deficiency
Society adopted the view that being alone means something is wrong
block_text:
Let’s look at where this idea actually comes from. For a long time, being alone was seen as a warning sign. If someone spent too much time by themselves, people assumed something was wrong. Maybe they were lonely. Maybe they couldn’t fit in. Maybe they were even a little unstable. This wasn’t just a casual opinion—it was baked into how people thought about mental health.

Early psychology didn’t help. In the past, psychologists often treated solitude as a symptom. If you liked being alone, it was seen as a red flag. The thinking was simple: humans are social animals, so wanting to be alone must mean you’re missing something. You’re lacking social skills. Or you’re avoiding life. Or you’re depressed. The message was clear—if you’re alone, you’re probably not okay.

This belief didn’t stay in textbooks. It spread everywhere. Schools, workplaces, even families started to see solitude as a problem to be fixed. If a child played alone, teachers worried. If an adult preferred quiet evenings, friends asked if they were alright. The assumption was always the same: solitude equals deficiency.

But here’s the thing—this view never really questioned why someone might choose solitude. It just labeled it. It didn’t ask what people actually felt inside. It didn’t consider that being alone could mean something different for different people. Instead, it turned solitude into a kind of social warning sign.

So, for decades, the story was simple: if you’re alone, you’re missing out. You’re not normal. And that story shaped how almost everyone saw themselves and others. But what if that story is wrong? What if solitude isn’t a problem at all? That’s where things start to get interesting.
